trees.title: A brake problem
trees.summary: The pedal feels different, you hear a noise when braking, or a brake warning light comes on.
trees.safety: Brakes are the car's primary safety system. Whenever you suspect a brake fluid leak, pads worn down to the metal, or a strong pull to one side when braking — don't keep driving.

n1.q: What do you feel or hear in the brakes?

options.label: The pedal feels soft, or sinks almost to the floor
The pedal is harder than usual, you need to press much harder
You hear a noise when braking — squealing or grinding
A brake warning light comes on, the car shakes or pulls to one side when braking

n2.q: Check the brake fluid level in the reservoir (engine off) — what's the state?

options.label: Within the normal range, but the pedal is still soft

n3.q: Do you see an oily, clear-to-yellowish fluid stain near one of the wheels, or under the car?

n6.q: What kind of noise, and when?

options.label: A thin, steady squeal, on every braking
Squealing only after rain or after the car has stood for a few hours, which disappears after a brake application or two
Heavy metallic grinding, like metal on metal
I forgot to release the parking brake
The parking brake is released, and the car shakes or pulses through the pedal when braking
The parking brake is released, and the car pulls to one side when braking
Only the warning light is on, with no unusual feeling in the pedal

r-servo.result: Suspected fault in the brake booster (servo) or its vacuum hose
r-servo.text: The pedal is meant to be relatively light to press, thanks to the brake booster. A pedal that's especially hard while the engine is running hints at a fault in the booster itself or the hose feeding it. Important: right after the engine is switched off, there's no vacuum in the booster, so the first few presses are deliberately harder — that's normal.
actions: Make sure the engine is running while you check how hard the pedal is.
If the pedal is hard even with the engine running, don't keep driving; go to a garage or call for a tow.

r-air-brakes.result: Probably air in the hydraulic brake system
r-air-brakes.text: The fluid level is normal, but the pedal is soft or “spongy” — a sign that air has got into the lines, usually after work on the brakes.
actions: Don't keep driving like this — braking may be only partial.
Go to a garage to bleed the air from the brake system.

r-fluid-leak.text: An oily, clear-to-yellowish stain near a wheel, together with a drop in the brake fluid level, is a leak from a sealed hydraulic system. A leak can progress to partial or complete loss of braking.
actions: Don't drive the car in this state.
If the fault is discovered while driving, stop at the first safe place and call for a tow.

r-pads-worn-fluid.result: Low fluid level, probably from worn brake pads
r-pads-worn-fluid.text: As the pads wear, the caliper pistons extend further, and the fluid level in the reservoir gradually drops even without a leak — a normal part of brake wear, needing a top-up and a check of the pad thickness.
actions: Top up brake fluid of the correct type to the mark, and go to a garage soon to have the pad thickness checked.
If the fluid level keeps dropping after topping up, this is probably a leak after all; don't drive.

r-wear-indicator.result: A wear reminder — the pads are nearing the end of their life
r-wear-indicator.text: Most cars have a small metal strip fitted in the pad, which produces a deliberate squeal once the pad reaches a minimum thickness — to warn before you reach the bare metal.
actions: Go to a garage to replace the pads soon.
Don't wait until the squeal turns into metallic grinding.

r-rust-glaze.result: Light rust on the disc — a temporary occurrence
r-rust-glaze.text: After rain, a wash, or when the car has stood for a few hours, a thin layer of rust forms on the disc's surface. The first few brake applications “clean” it off, which is why you hear a squeal that disappears quickly.
actions: No action is needed if the squeal disappears after a brake application or two.
If the squeal continues beyond that, go and check the pad thickness.

r-pads-metal.result: Brake pads worn down to the metal
r-pads-metal.text: Metallic grinding when braking, like metal rubbing on metal, means the pad has worn completely away and its metal backing is hitting the disc directly — this harms braking effectiveness and also damages the disc.
actions: Drive with maximum care and go straight to a garage, without delay.
If this is happening on both axles, consider a tow instead of continuing to drive.

r-parking-brake-on.result: The parking brake wasn't fully released
r-parking-brake-on.text: Driving with the parking brake applied, even partially, heats up the brakes and wears them quickly, and also lights the warning light on the dashboard.
actions: Release the parking brake fully before driving.
If the light stays on after releasing it, go and check the brake fluid level.

r-warped-disc.result: Suspected brake disc that isn't an even thickness
r-warped-disc.text: Shaking or pulsing in the pedal when braking, mainly from high speed, points to a disc that has warped or worn unevenly.
actions: Go to a garage for a check, and to have the disc skimmed or replaced.
Until it's repaired, leave a bigger braking gap.

r-pull-braking.result: The car pulls to one side when braking — suspected partial failure in one brake
r-pull-braking.text: Pulling to one side only when braking, and not during normal driving, hints at a stuck caliper, a blocked brake hose, or a brake that has seized on one side — braking isn't split evenly between the sides.
actions: Drive with maximum care to the nearest garage, and avoid sharp braking if possible.
For more detail: [[tree:car-pulls-to-side|the car pulls to one side]].
